title: Insurance stocks: how to analyze insurance companies
description: Insurance stocks run on two engines: underwriting and the float. Calculate the combined ratio, read the reserves, value insurers with P/B and ROE.
author: AK1A Research Lab
body:
Insurance stocks are shares in companies selling protection against future losses — a business built on a temporal inversion: the customer pays today for a service delivered only when damage occurs. Premiums are booked before costs are known; the result runs on two engines — the technical, premiums against claims, and the financial, the return on money while waiting. AK1A's universe carries three variants of the machinery: Allianz and Sampo pure insurance groups, Berkshire Hathaway an insurance-led conglomerate. Between them lies insurance analysis: combined ratio, float, reserves.

This guide walks the mechanisms with the universe's own numbers. As always: education in method, never advice about individual stocks.

## What are insurance stocks — the business with two engines

Insurance divides in two: property and casualty — homes, vehicles, companies, claims striking unevenly — and life and pension, where actuarial tables give slower calculability. Allianz runs both; Sampo, post-Nordea, is a pure P&C group with If P&C, Topdanmark and Hastings. P&C premiums are rewritten yearly — the customer base pays again every twelfth month — a revenue base like a subscription, a structure [revenue stability analysis](/kurser/v12-intaktsstabilitet) captures.

Claims arise from weather, accidents and fire — not stock-market swings. Sampo's beta of 0.24 in the universe's data sits below Coca-Cola's 0.34: an earnings machine whose income is no stock-market product. That correlation — not the sector name — makes insurance interesting in [diversification](/kurser/pf-03-diversifiering).

## Combined ratio — the technical thermometer

The sector's key ratio is the combined ratio: claims plus operating costs, divided by premium income. Below 100 means technical profit on the underwriting itself; above 100, claims and administration cost more than premiums collect. Simplified example: 100 in premiums, 74 in claims, 22 in costs — combined ratio 96, four left per hundred as technical profit. With 82 in claims instead: 104, a technical loss of four. But the second engine enters: four percent return on the 100 float gives four in financial income — zero despite the loss.

The two pure groups show the spread. If P&C landed 2025 at 83.6 — 0.7 percentage points better than the year before — with a technical result of 1,485 million euro, up twelve percent; Allianz's P&C business noted 92.2 against 93.4. Per hundred in premiums If keeps 16.4, Allianz 7.8 — more than twice the technical margin on the same business. The difference is structural: Sampo's target is a combined ratio below 85 year after year. The number cycles — soft competition presses premiums, catastrophe years harden them — a [moat](/kurser/mt-01-vad-ar-en-moat) tested through the cycle, not one year.

## The float — customer money put to work

Between payment in and payment out lies the float: customer money under management. Allianz carries cash of 136.0 billion euro against 33.7 billion in traditional interest-bearing debt — cash alone exceeds the debt four times; Sampo 18.16 against 2.55, more than seven times. Formally the policyholders' money, in practice working for the shareholders while waiting. A float that grows while the combined ratio holds below 100 is negatively interest-bearing funding.

Berkshire Hathaway is the float's extreme — and its analysis trap. The result series 2022–2025 runs −22.8, 96.2, 89.0 and 67.0 billion dollars: swings predominantly unrealized stock-portfolio value changes, not the insurance business — even 2022's minus is stock-market weather. A P/E of 12.6 on that denominator says more about the market's year than the float machine — the [P/E walkthrough](/kurser/km-009-pe)'s warning, magnified. Same note on Allianz's free cash flow yield of 16.7 percent: customer money flowing through the balance sheet, not cash free to distribute — the craft is [cash flow analysis](/kurser/km-003-kassaflodesanalysen).

## The reserves — the balance sheet's estimates

Insurance's hardest item is invisible in the income statement: reserves for claims occurred but not yet paid. A December house fire can take years to settle — the company must today set aside what it will cost. Reserving too little shows profit today, loss tomorrow, when older years' claims prove dearer than expected; a recurring deficiency in prior years' reserve development is the sector's clearest warning pattern.

The reserves also explain why debt measures need reservation. The universe's debt-to-equity — 0.51 for Allianz, 0.35 for Sampo — covers traditional interest-bearing debt; insurance obligations sit outside. Head-on against a manufacturer they mislead — why [ROIC numbers](/blogg/roic-den-glomda-nyckeltalen-v11) are hard to compare across the financial line. Insurance stocks are therefore valued on equity and return — the bank-analysis convention: [P/B together with ROE](/kurser/v05-pb). The universe's numbers: Sampo at P/B 3.38 with ROE 24.1 percent, Allianz 2.47 with 19.6, against the finance branch median 2.47 and 15.3 — both well above the midpoint. Turn the fraction as with the P/E's earnings yield — ROE divided by P/B is the return on the booked capital you pay for: 7.1 percent Sampo, 7.9 Allianz, suddenly comparable with an interest rate. [What ROE measures](/blogg/vad-ar-roe) and [when P/B is compared right](/blogg/pb-tal-nar-jamfor-man-bokvarde-ratt) go through both measures' pitfalls.

## The interest rate, the record year and the multiple

The interest rate acts twice — antipole of the bank's simple coupling. A higher rate makes the float more valuable: the return on customer money rises. The same rate presses the value of the bonds the reserves sit in. Which effect dominates depends on horizon and portfolio — [the pricing of interest](/kurser/km-054-ranta) is mandatory reading, and the maturities sit in the notes to [the annual report](/blogg/sa-laser-du-en-svensk-arsredovisning).

Multiple reading has two traps. The first is the record year: Sampo trades at P/E 14.7 — but 2025 was the group's best year (net result 1,998 million euro, up 73 percent), and consensus normalizes downward: forward 16.2 above trailing 14.7, the peak-base-year pattern. PEG becomes meaningless on such a base. The second is the one-off: Allianz's P/E 14.6 carries a divestment gain from the Indian life engagement — the result before one-offs sits around 2.1 billion euro lower, so the normalized multiple is higher. The discipline of [quarterly report reading](/kurser/km-006-kvartalsrapporten) — separate the recurring from the one-off — applies at annual level too.

Both groups carry dividends: Allianz pays 17.10 euro per share — 3.8 percent yield, 55 percent payout ratio, raised from 11.40 euro in three years, around 14.5 percent per year; Sampo 0.36 euro, 3.7 percent, essentially the same ratio. Depth: [the dividend course](/kurser/ud-06-svenska-utdelningsaktier), [equity and dividends](/kurser/km-005-eget-kapital-utdelningar), and the branch median in [the sector median walkthrough](/blogg/branschmedianer-akm2).

## How to read the report — five points

- **The combined ratio and its parts.** Claims ratio and cost ratio each tell where improvement comes from — lower claims is quality, lower costs can be cuts with service as the price.
- **Reserve development for prior years.** Outcome against earlier years' reserving; recurring deficiency is more serious than a single quarter above 100.
- **The financial result and the investments.** Return on the float, bonds against alternatives, maturities — interest sensitivity lives here.
- **The capital coverage.** The supervisor's solvency measure — Allianz reported 218 percent at year-end — governs the room for dividends.
- **Dividend and targets.** Payout ratio against target, and whether the combined ratio target held through the cycle.

## The summary

- Two engines: technical result (premiums against claims) and financial result (the float) — a combined ratio below 100 with a growing float is the machinery's heart.
- Underwriting quality is measured in the combined ratio: If 83.6 against Allianz 92.2 in 2025 — 16.4 against 7.8 left per hundred in premiums.
- The float shows in the balance sheet: Allianz cash 136.0 billion euro against 33.7 in traditional debt; Sampo 18.16 against 2.55 — customer money at work.
- Debt measures cover only traditional debt — reserves sit outside; value with P/B and ROE, and check prior years' reserve development.
- The interest rate acts twice (float return up, bond values down); record years and one-offs make P/E and PEG misleading unless normalized.

Continuation: [The finance sector](/kurser/se-06-finanssektorn) in course form; [the complete guide to Swedish stock analysis](/blogg/komplett-guide-svensk-aktieanalys-2026) for context.
